title: Classical simulation of amplitude-damped bucket-brigade quantum random access memories via predictable branch evolution
authors: Zhao-Yun Chen, Ming-Yang Tan, Sheng Zhang, Peng Wang, Yun-Jie Wang, Guo-Ping Guo
abstract: Classical simulation of quantum random access memory (QRAM) under noise can be accelerated dramatically by branch pruning: noise histories are sampled as trajectory ensembles, and good branches, whose routing paths avoid every sampled fault, need not be evolved because their final states are analytically predictable. Under amplitude damping this predictability is not automatic, because the no-jump operator $K_0$ acts on every branch at every time slice. Here we give a complete account of damping-channel predictability in bucket-brigade QRAM simulation, for both qutrit and qubit encodings. For the qutrit encoding, $K_0$ is diagonal in the node basis, and the wait state $|W\rangle$ is its fixed point, so a good branch follows the noiseless orbit up to a scalar attenuation. In the qubit encoding, phase-kickback memory fetching between two Hadamard walls makes $K_0$ no longer diagonal, yet the resulting structure is exactly solvable in closed form. Conditional on no jump, the in-branch infidelity of a good branch is second order in the damping rate $γ$, with coherent leakage $\sim n^2γ^2/4$ per data qubit, and the closed form captures it without approximation. We also revise the pruning criterion for the qubit encoding. The resulting algorithm evolves only the bad branches plus one reference branch and shares every other cost with the full evolution it replaces. It is validated by end-to-end benchmarks with pruned-over-full speedups up to $285\times$ and by trajectory-level tests confirming every closed form to machine precision.
summary: This work presents a novel, highly efficient classical simulation technique for noisy Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) using branch pruning. By analytically predicting the evolution of 'good' quantum branches, the authors achieve substantial speedups over full simulations. This advances the practical simulation capabilities for quantum memory architectures under realistic noise models.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of developing a fast and accurate classical simulation for Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) operating under noise, specifically amplitude damping.
main_result: They achieve significant computational speedups (up to 285x) by developing a branch pruning technique that analytically predicts the final states of 'good' quantum branches.
method: The core method is a quantum-trajectory Monte Carlo simulation enhanced by branch pruning, which avoids full evolution for predictable paths.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a bucket-brigade QRAM, analyzed using both qubit and qutrit encodings. Noise includes amplitude damping and depolarizing faults.
key_observables: End-state fidelities, speedup factors (pruned-over-full), and the in-branch infidelity (second order in the damping rate $\gamma$).
important_parameters: Amplitude damping strength ($\gamma$), address size ($n$), and noise probability ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The predictability of good branches under amplitude damping was not automatic, requiring novel analytical treatments for both qutrit and qubit cases.
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually shows the pruned simulation for qubit-encoded QRAM using the XOR mirror. Figure 4 plots the speedup and evolved fraction versus noise level and address size.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for efficient simulation under damping, then details the analytical predictability for qutrit and qubit encodings, proposes a revised pruning criterion, and finally validates the entire algorithm using end-to-end benchmarks and cross-checks against density matrix evolution.
why_interesting: The techniques developed for analytically predicting quantum evolution along specific, noise-avoiding paths are highly relevant for simulating open quantum systems where full time evolution is intractable.
